meta.title: Detecting Lunar Craters at Scale
meta.authorsHtml: Patrick Bauer<sup>∗</sup><sup>1,2,3</sup>, Marius Schwinning<sup>2</sup>, Florian Renk<sup>2</sup>, Andreas Weinmann<sup>4</sup>, Melanie Siegel<sup>3</sup>, Hichem Snoussi<sup>1</sup>

abstract: The reliable detection of lunar craters is a common research topic in machine learning-driven object detection. It is also of practical interest given the focus of the European Space Agency on planned lunar missions. There are many sites of interest on the lunar surface, and an automated system that can detect as many craters as possible would be valuable for observing and analyzing potential landing sites. Nevertheless, automated crater detection algorithms based on deep learning methods struggle with challenging image conditions, such as rugged terrain and different illumination that affect the appearance of craters. Additionally, some detection models fail to generalize when faced with distinct variations in crater shape and size, and are unable to detect craters that are only a few pixels in size. In this paper, we build upon the OWLv2 framework to introduce a multi-scale crater detection approach capable of robustly identifying craters of diverse sizes and shapes across varying illumination conditions. We contribute a system that processes full Calibrated Data Record images from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera and outputs detection results that cover the entire image.

blocks.html: Since the European Space Agency (ESA) held its Ministerial Council in Bremen, Germany, in November 2025, where the 23 ESA Member States committed the largest contribution at 22.3 billion Euros in the history of the ESA [1], the focus on space innovations — both software and hardware — has reached a new high. Besides other major programs such as the European Resilience from Space initiative, the ESA plans missions to land on the Moon with the Argonaut lunar lander programme [2]. Therefore, the reliable detection of lunar craters to support safe and soft landings becomes a major research topic of interest and is more important now than ever. Driven by this goal, we contribute a multi-scale crater detection pipeline applied to full Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) Calibrated Data Record (CDR) images using a reliable lunar crater detector [3], that is capable of detecting craters of various sizes and shapes and under different illumination conditions. Crater detection algorithms (CDAs) can usually be divided into manual and automatic approaches, with the latter being superior due to the labour costs and error-proneness of manual labelling approaches [4]. The most prominent approaches in automatic CDAs rely on deep learning methods. Several of these approaches are based on variants of the You Only Look Once (YOLO) model, e.g. Nan et al. [5], Zuo et al. [6] and La Grassa et al. [7]. In recent years, Transformer-based models yielded promising results in various computer vision tasks. With Crater-DETR [8], the authors applied a variant of the detection Transformer (DETR) to the task of crater detection achieving high accuracy. Giannakis et al. [9] applied the Segment Anything Model (SAM) for crater detection and achieved good visual results, even without finetuning it on a crater database. The authors of [10], showed that, also without fine-tuning, the OWLv2 model [11] can become a promising crater detector by a few-shot detection approach combined with modifying OWLv2’s similarity score calculation method, while omitting the text Transformer. A recent approach introduced a crater detection model based on fine-tuning the pre-trained OWLv2 model [3]. Specifically, the authors fine-tuned OWLv2 by utilizing the labelled data of the IMPACT project [12], by inserting new trainable parameters to the model based on the parameter efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) strategy with low rank adaptation (LoRA) [13]. Henceforth, we refer to this model as Crater-OWLv2. Its inference-pipeline follows the zero-shot object detection principle: The word “crater” is processed with the frozen text Transformer module, which yields a high-dimensional embedding. Meanwhile, an image is processed using the fine-tuned ViT in OWLv2. The output embeddings of the text Transformer and ViT are then projected onto the class and box heads, respectively. If the cosine similarity between a certain image region — defined by its bounding box and its class embedding — and the text embedding exceeds a certain threshold, the object is classified as a crater. Crater-OWLv2 already achieve promising crater detection results, cf. Figure 1. It has strong generalization capabilities in detecting diverse type of craters. However, we emphasize a limitation. Although Crater-OWLv2 can detect small craters well, we have noticed that, in some cases, the model does not detect craters that exceed a certain size relative to the image size. We argue, that this may be due to a learned bias towards craters smaller than ∼30% of the image size, as the underlying training data from IMPACT [12] mostly contains craters of small sizes. However, if we consider the same crater in a larger image, i.e. one that covers a larger physical area containing the undetected crater, the model is able to detect it. Nevertheless, we can overcome this size bias using a multi-scale crater detection pipeline. As outlined by Fairweather et al. [14], some craters across image tiles cannot be detected due to the image resolution, for example, tiling may cut craters in pieces when inference is run on NAC CDR image tiles. That means, even without the bias towards crater size, a multi-scale approach combined with a merging technique is required to detect both small and large craters. We have therefore adapted and modified the pyramid approach described by Fairweather et al. [14] to contribute a pyramid-based detection and merging technique. This enables the precise detection of craters of various sizes on different scales, ensuring that as many craters as possible are identified given any LROC NAC CDR image.

blocks.html: The Crater-OWLv2 model [3] yields a robust crater detector capable of generalizing well across various lunar imaging conditions. We use the model to develop a multi-scale pipeline, detecting different sized craters based on the image scale and using an overall merging technique to map all craters in the full CDR image. The images used for this paper are downloaded from the Planetary Data System archive (https://pds.lroc.asu.edu/data/).

Minderer et al. [11] introduced the OWLv2 model, that is capable of zero-shot object detection. This means that the pre-trained model can detect objects that were not necessarily seen during the training process. The principle works by prompting objects of interest that are described in text and processed through the text Transformer, while an image is processed through the ViT. If the object is present in the image, the model can detect it and mark its location in the image with a bounding box. While this approach is effective for everyday-scenery images and objects, large pre-trained models such as OWLv2 typically perform poorly when applied to remote sensing images without fine-tuning due to a large domain gap [15]. For example, Luo et al. [16] addressed this issue by fine-tuning SAM on remote sensing imagery. While OWLv2 initially struggled to detect craters, efficient fine-tuning by inserting new trainable parameters into the model based on LoRA yielded a reliable crater detector in Crater-OWLv2 [3]. We use Crater-OWLv2 alongside a multi-scale detection pipeline and merging technique to process full NAC CDR images selected out-of-distribution. This enables us to detect craters of various sizes and shapes.

blocks.title: Multi-Scale Approach for Full NAC CDR Crater Detection

blocks.html: The general idea is that, depending on the scale, we want to detect craters of different sizes w.r.t. the image size: small craters (4–25 pixels) on a small scale, medium craters (25–100 pixels) on a medium scale, and large craters (>100 pixels) on a large scale and then merge them into the overall CDR image. We distinguish between crater sizes based on the pixel scale rather than the actual physical size in meter, which we can derive by utilizing the image metadata. The pyramidal approach is built on the method of Fairweather et al. [14] and designed as follows: First, we take a full NAC CDR image, which typically measures 52,224 × 5,064 pixels, and divide it into tiles of size 5,064 × 5,064. This approach would obviously cause edge problems if a large crater was intersected by the tiling. Therefore, we use a stride of 4,642. Each tile is processed iteratively by following the scheme shown in Figure 2. Starting with the tiles of size 5,064 × 5,064, we divide them into 676 overlapping tiles to mitigate intersections at borders, each measuring 211×211 pixels. This results in an overlap of 12 pixels between subsequent tiles. At this scale, the smallest possible craters are detected, since as a pre-processing step, OWLv2 increases the size of each crater by a factor of 4.55 by resizing each image to 960×960 pixels. This enables Crater-OWLv2 to detect small craters at this scale, which are referred to as level 0 detections. Level 1 detections, which serve as a small-tomedium-sized detector, are obtained by downsampling the original image tile to half its size (i.e. 2,532 pixels). We also generate 211×211-sized overlapping tiles with an overlap of 24 pixels, totalling 196 tiles. Repeating this process by downsampling the original image to a quarter of its size (1,266 pixels) yields 46 level 2 tiles, each with an overlap of 48 pixels, for medium-to-large-sized craters. Level 3 uses the original tile, downsampled to 633×633 pixels to detect large craters. At each level, we run the inference with Crater-OWLv2 and keep all possible crater detection if the cosine similarity between the image class embeddings and the text embedding exceeds a threshold t = 0.30.

The first step yielded detections on all 5,064×5,064 tiles of the full CDR image at different scales. To merge them, we first considered the intra-tile detections, i.e. all detections at each level inside its corresponding 5,064-sized tile. First, we penalize all bounding boxes with coordinates that would leave the 211-sized tiles by multiplying the confidence scores by 0.2. Since, due to the overlap, the detections are fully inside consecutive horizontal or vertical tiles without an image border intersecting the corresponding craters. Multiple detections in resulting overlapping regions are handled with non-maximum-suppression (NMS). NMS is a technique based on intersection over union (IoU) and retains only the detection with the highest score when multiple boxes cover the same area. To do so, we apply an IoU threshold of 0.2. After this, we map them back to the original pixel space of 5,064 and retain all detections at each level. We then apply a size threshold to the level detections to merge them. Level 0 keeps boxes with a pixel size (relative to the full CDR image) of [4, 16]; level 1 of [12, 54]; level 2 of [48, 126]; and level 3, larger than 120. To merge the craters across vertically adjacent 5,064-pixel tiles, we select only detections whose center lies within the overlapping regions and also apply NMS with an IoU threshold of 0.2, retaining the highest-scoring craters.

We show the results on 8 different NAC CDR stripes in Figure 3. Rather than using rectangular bounding boxes, we transform each bounding box into its inscribed ellipse. We emphasize that a significant proportion of the elliptical detections cover the entire crater and do not result in misaligned ellipses. Overall, our qualitative evaluation in Figure 3 underlines the high quality of detection of craters of various sizes and shapes by utilizing Crater-OWLv2 combined with the multi-scale approach. A majority of craters are detected in each image. The score threshold is set to t = 0.3 in each image, except for M1517845850LC (centered at ∼80◦N), where the detection score threshold for the level 0 detections is set to t = 0.95. Otherwise, we observed some false positives, particularly in shadowed regions, due to extreme illumination conditions that can occur in the polar regions of the Moon [17]. Notably, the detections in M185589205RC suggest that the model generalizes well, as it can detect craters from an off-nadir view, in which craters appear more elliptical. Further, we note that Crater-OWLv2 paired with the pyramidal detection approach yields good detection of very small craters, i.e. those between 4 and 16 pixels. We emphasize that a majority of these detections are indeed true positives, although in some cases it is difficult to decide whether a certain feature might be a crater or not. While some detections fit the corresponding crater very well, the model sometimes predicts the crater’s shape incorrectly and only covers part of it. This is especially the case when the low-lighted part of the crater is circular or when the terrain is difficult and rugged. We note that some very large craters may be falsely not detected.

In this paper, we used Crater-OWLv2 to detect craters at scale. We developed a detection algorithm based on a pyramid approach with a merging technique to generate a pipeline for detecting as many craters as possible on various NAC CDR images. The qualitative evaluation shows that this method is capable of detecting craters on full NAC CDR images while a few craters — especially very large ones — are false negatives. The pipeline is applicable to various lunar image conditions. In some cases, only the shadowed part of the crater is detected rather than the entire crater. Furthermore, we intend to address the issue of very large craters going undetected in future by using a semi-supervised learning approach. This will involve using a pseudo-labelled dataset generated by this pipeline. In the future, we also aim to make detections of craters along with its georeferenced coordinates public, so that other researches can use the data to train and evaluate deep learning models.
